n: A serious dispute arose. Teachers from Judea insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved — in effect, become Jews first.

f.w: Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses

n: Paul and Barnabas argued strongly against this. The Antioch church sent them to Jerusalem so the apostles and elders could settle the question — the Church’s proper way to resolve doctrine.

f.w: unto the apostles and elders about this question

n: On the way they told congregations in Phoenicia and Samaria about the Gentile conversions, and everyone rejoiced.

f.g: Phoenicia, the coastal region of modern Lebanon.

n: The Jerusalem church and its leaders welcomed them warmly, and they reported all that God had done through them.
But some believers who had been Pharisees insisted Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the full law of Moses. They had accepted Jesus but still held tightly to their old framework.

f.w: the sect of the Pharisees which believed
f.g: Jewish Christians who came from the strict Pharisee party.

n: The apostles and elders met in council to consider the matter carefully. This gathering is often called the Jerusalem Council (about AD 49).
After much debate, Peter — the senior apostle — stood up. He reminded them that God had chosen him to bring the gospel to the Gentiles first, at Cornelius’s house.
God, who sees the heart, showed his approval of the Gentiles by giving them the Holy Ghost just as he had to the Jewish believers.
God made no distinction between Jew and Gentile, cleansing their hearts through faith — not through circumcision.
Why test God by placing a burden on converts that even we Jews could never fully carry? Peter calls the ritual law a heavy yoke.

f.g: Test God — challenge what he has already made clear.

n: Peter’s great conclusion: both Jews and Gentiles are saved the same way — through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.

f.w: through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved

n: The assembly fell silent and listened as Barnabas and Paul described the miracles God had worked among the Gentiles — more evidence of God’s approval.
Then James spoke. This is James the Lord’s brother, who presided over the church in Jerusalem.
James summarized Peter’s testimony: God had begun gathering a people for his name from among the Gentiles. “Simeon” is the Hebrew form of Simon, Peter’s birth name.

f.g: A Hebrew form of Simon — Peter’s original name.

n: James shows that this agrees with the prophets. Scripture and revelation confirm each other.
He quotes Amos: God would rebuild David’s fallen “tabernacle” or tent — the house and kingdom of David — restoring what had collapsed.

f.w: build again the tabernacle of David

f.g: Tent or dwelling — here David’s royal house and kingdom.

n: The purpose: that all people — including Gentiles who take God’s name upon them — might seek the Lord. The restoration of Israel would bless the whole world.

f.w: upon whom my name is called

n: God has known his plans from the very beginning. Including the Gentiles was no afterthought.

f.w: from the beginning of the world

n: James gives his judgment: don’t burden Gentile converts with requirements God hasn’t given. “Sentence” means decision or verdict.

Instead, ask them to avoid four things that would especially offend Jewish believers or tie them to pagan practices: food sacrificed to idols, sexual immorality, meat from strangled animals, and consuming blood.

f.g: Defilement from pagan worship, especially eating sacrificed meat.

n: Moses’ law is read every Sabbath in synagogues everywhere, so these basic courtesies would help Gentile and Jewish believers live and eat together in peace.
The apostles, elders, and whole church agreed. They chose two respected leaders, Judas Barsabas and Silas, to go with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch.

f.g: Also called Silvanus; he soon became Paul’s missionary companion.

n: They wrote an official letter to the Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, where the dispute had arisen.

f.g: Region in southeastern Asia Minor; Paul’s home province, with Tarsus its chief city.

n: The letter clearly states that those who demanded circumcision had not been sent by the Church leaders. Their teaching had unsettled the converts.

f.w: to whom we gave no such commandment

n: The council was united, and they chose to send official representatives alongside their beloved Barnabas and Paul.
The letter honors Paul and Barnabas as men who had risked their lives for Jesus Christ.
Judas and Silas would confirm the message in person, so no one could doubt its authenticity.
A key phrase: “it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.” The decision was made by revelation through united Church councils, not mere human opinion.

f.w: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us

n: The letter lists the four requirements and ends with a warm farewell. “Meats” means food of any kind; here, meat offered in pagan sacrifices.
The messengers returned to Antioch, gathered the congregation, and delivered the letter.
The believers rejoiced at its encouraging message. They were free from the burden of the old ritual law.
Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, gave many words of encouragement and strengthened the church.
After some time, the Antioch church sent them back to Jerusalem with blessings of peace.
Silas decided to stay in Antioch. Many ancient manuscripts lack this verse, but it explains why Silas is available for Paul’s next journey.
Paul and Barnabas kept teaching in Antioch, along with many other teachers.
Later, Paul suggested revisiting the cities from their first mission to see how the new believers were doing. Good missionaries follow up.
Barnabas wanted to bring his cousin John Mark again.
Paul refused because Mark had left them partway through the first mission. Paul feared he might not be reliable.

f.w: who departed from them from Pamphylia

n: The disagreement was so sharp that they parted ways. Even good leaders can disagree. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus — and Paul later spoke warmly of Mark.

f.g: Greek paroxysmos — a sharp, heated disagreement.

n: Paul chose Silas as his new companion, and the church sent them off commending them to God’s grace. This begins Paul’s second missionary journey.
Paul and Silas traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the branches along the way.
